# Research pass 1 — Achilles/lower-limb resilience and the marathon/ultra build

> Generated by Claude's Research tool, 21 September 2026, from a prompt written in the
> "STRAVA x CLAUDE" project. Evidence grades were assigned by the tool, not by independent
> appraisal. Most cited studies were named in the text without links and have not been
> individually checked. See `references.md`.

*This report is structured to split into two reference documents: Part One (Achilles/lower-limb resilience and load management) and Part Two (endurance training structure and the marathon build). Each substantive recommendation is tagged for evidence strength: **well-supported** (systematic reviews/RCTs/consensus), **reasonable inference** (extrapolated from good evidence), or **practitioner heuristic** (coaching practice where research is thin).*

## TL;DR
- **The single highest-priority change is a structured, progressive calf/Achilles loading programme run alongside deliberately separated easy and hard running.** The athlete has never directly loaded the calf until August 2026, and his recurrent flares come from volume and intensity rising together on an under-prepared tendon. Strength training is the best-evidenced injury-prevention tool available — Lauersen et al. (BJSM 2014) reported strength training reduced overuse injuries by 47% (RR 0.527, 95% CI 0.373–0.746) and total injuries to under a third, while stretching did nothing.
- **His own 3:13 data replicated the strongest finding in the endurance literature:** shifting from short fast intervals to longer threshold reps plus genuinely easy running (a pyramidal distribution) is what recreational marathoners respond to. The fix for sub-3 is more easy volume and more threshold work — not more grey-zone running compressed into 4:45–5:15/km.
- **Sub-3 is realistic from his engine (3:13 PB, 17:55 5k, 1:29 HM) but requires ~55–70 km/week peak volume sustained for 12–16 weeks,** which collides directly with his Achilles history. The resolution: build tendon capacity FIRST over the next 3–6 months, keep a permanent year-round base, and only trigger the sharpening block once he can tolerate the volume pain-free.

# PART ONE — ACHILLES AND LOWER-LIMB LOAD TOLERANCE

## 1.1 What kind of Achilles problem is this (and the diagnosis caveat)
**Evidence strength: well-supported for the general classification; the individual diagnosis is unconfirmed and needs in-person assessment.**

The athlete has **not** had a formal diagnosis. Nothing below replaces an in-person assessment by a sports physiotherapist or sports physician, which is genuinely warranted here given 2.5+ years of recurrent lower-limb symptoms, a December 2025 report of "intense heel > ankle pain", and a significant July 2026 flare. The value of an in-person assessment is (a) confirming mid-portion vs insertional location, (b) ruling out differentials (posterior tibialis tendinopathy, plantaris involvement, Haglund's/retrocalcaneal bursitis, bone stress injury), and (c) baseline capacity testing.

Achilles tendinopathy splits into two presentations that matter for loading:
- **Mid-portion** (pain 2–6 cm above the heel): 60–75% of cases, more common in active runners. Tolerates stretch/dorsiflexion loading well.
- **Insertional** (pain at the bone–tendon junction at the heel): roughly a quarter of cases, more common in older/less active people, and less responsive to standard non-surgical treatment. Critically, it is aggravated by **compression** — deep heel-drops off a step (full dorsiflexion) can worsen it, so insertional cases are loaded in a reduced range (flat ground, avoiding end-range dorsiflexion).

The December 2025 "heel > ankle" description raises the possibility of an insertional or heel component, which would change exercise prescription (avoid end-range dorsiflexion). This is exactly why the location needs confirming before heavy heel-drop work.

**Natural history of a 9+-month on-and-off tendinopathy:** this is now a **persistent/recurrent** presentation, not an acute one. Persistent tendinopathy is characterised by a propensity to chronicity, prolonged recovery, and a weak relationship between tendon structure on imaging and symptoms — pain does not track tissue "damage" closely, and altered central pain processing may contribute to why symptoms recur. The practical implication: he should expect a months-long capacity-building project, judge progress by function and load tolerance rather than by being pain-free, and accept that some symptoms during loading are acceptable (see 1.3).

## 1.2 Loading protocols: what actually works
**Evidence strength: well-supported that loading works and is first-line; contested which specific protocol is best.**

The core evidence-based message is that progressive loading is the first-line treatment and that **no single loading protocol is clearly superior**. A living systematic review with network meta-analysis (van der Vlist et al., BJSM 2021) found no convincing evidence that any adjunct (shockwave, injections) outperforms exercise alone, and recommended exercise monotherapy be offered for at least 3 months before considering an adjunct.

The main options:
- **Eccentric (Alfredson):** 3×15 heel-drops, both straight- and bent-knee, twice daily, 7 days/week, 12 weeks (≈180 reps/day). Landmark evidence, but high time burden and lower compliance.
- **Heavy Slow Resistance (HSR):** the Beyer et al. (AJSM 2015) protocol — 3 exercises (seated/bent-knee calf raise, standing straight-knee barbell calf raise, leg-press calf raise), 3×/week, 6-second reps (3s concentric/3s eccentric), progressing **15RM (wk1) → 12RM (wk2–3) → 10RM (wk4–5) → 8RM (wk6–8) → 6RM (wk9–12)**, 2–3 min rest between sets. In the RCT (n=58, chronic mid-portion, Level 1) both eccentric and HSR produced equal, lasting improvements (VISA-A ~74 at 12 weeks, ~87 at 52 weeks), but HSR had **higher compliance (92% vs 78%)** and greater 12-week satisfaction. Total tendon-loading time was ~41 min/week for HSR vs ~308 min/week for the eccentric protocol.
- **Isometrics:** widely promoted for immediate pain relief, but **this is the most contested claim in the area**. The original enthusiasm rested on a very small (n=6) patellar-tendon study (Rio et al.); subsequent work, including a quasi-RCT specifically in Achilles tendinopathy (van der Vlist et al. 2020), found isometrics did **not** provide reliable immediate analgesia, with heterogeneous "responder/non-responder" patterns. A systematic review concluded isometric exercise is not superior to isotonic for chronic tendinopathy. Verdict: isometrics are a reasonable low-irritability starting option and may help some individuals, but should not be sold as a guaranteed pain switch.

**For this athlete, HSR is the best fit:** it aligns with his existing twice-weekly gym habit and barbell access, has the best compliance data, and builds the load capacity he is missing. This is the highest-value single intervention in the whole report.

**Timeline to expect:** the longitudinal meta-analysis (Murphy et al., Sports Med 2018) found a mean VISA-A improvement of ~21 points at 12 weeks, with meaningful change detectable from ~2 weeks. Early improvement (first 2–4 weeks) is largely neural/pain-modulation, not structural — tendon structure does not change in 2 weeks and muscle hypertrophy takes 4+ weeks. Expect a 3-month horizon for the loading programme to bite, and a longer runway to full running capacity.

## 1.3 Monitoring and progression: the pain-monitoring model
**Evidence strength: well-supported (RCT-backed).**

Silbernagel's pain-monitoring model (Silbernagel, Thomeé, Eriksson & Karlsson, *American Journal of Sports Medicine* 2007;35(6):897–906; RCT, n=38, Level 1 evidence) is the validated framework and directly applicable. Its rules:
- Pain during and after loading (including running) is **acceptable up to about 5/10** on a 0–10 scale.
- It must settle to baseline by the next morning.
- It must not progressively climb week to week.
- **Morning stiffness and first-steps pain are the key monitoring signal** — increasing morning symptoms mean the previous day's load was too much.

In the RCT, runners who continued running under this model did as well as those who rested for the first 6 weeks — "no significant differences in the rate of improvements were found between the groups." He does not need to stop running to rehab; he needs to regulate it. This matters for adherence and mood, which he explicitly values.

## 1.4 Calf/plantarflexor capacity: benchmarks and loading
**Evidence strength: well-supported for the loading forces and test protocols; benchmarks are reasonable inference (norms vary by protocol).**

Why this matters: the Achilles sees very high loads in running. Komi's in-vivo buckle-transducer measurements (Komi, *J Biomech* 1990) recorded Achilles tendon forces as high as **~9 kN, ~12.5× body weight** at the top end (a single-subject maximal value; neuromusculoskeletal modelling gives lower means of ~2–4× BW, so treat "6–12× BW" as a methodology-dependent range). The **soleus is the single biggest contributor** to Achilles force and provides the majority of vertical support during running — which is why **bent-knee (soleus-biased) calf work matters as much as straight-knee (gastrocnemius) work**. If the calf fatigues, the tendon and passive structures absorb more of that load. His gym log shows he never trained this directly — a clear, correctable gap that plausibly underlies both the Achilles flares and the backyard-ultra "legs won't restart / feet destroyed" failure.

**Testing/benchmarks (single-leg heel-raise to fatigue, ~30/min, straight knee, on a slight incline):**
- Silbernagel's linear-encoder test (Silbernagel et al., *KSSTA* 2010) measures repetitions, height, AND **total work** (vertical displacement × body weight). Repetition count alone overstates recovery — in her rupture data, repetitions recovered to 95% limb symmetry at 12 months while WORK was still only 76%. **Judge recovery on work and height, not just reps.**
- Return-to-sport target: **Limb Symmetry Index within ~10–20% of the uninjured side** (LSI ≥ 80–90%).
- Normative context (Hébert-Losier et al., *Physiotherapy* 2017, n=566, 10° incline): median ~23–24 reps across all adults; a fit ~30-year-old male should be capable of roughly 30+ per side. Norms are highly protocol-dependent (incline, cadence, height), so **use his own left-vs-right symmetry as the primary gauge** rather than absolute cutoffs.

**Loading dose to build capacity:** follow the HSR progression above (15RM→6RM over 12 weeks, 3×/week) for the rehab/capacity phase, always training BOTH bent-knee (soleus) and straight-knee (gastrocnemius) variations. For maintenance thereafter, 2×/week heavy calf work is sufficient. This slots directly into his two weekly gym sessions.

## 1.5 Foot and lower-limb resilience for ultra-duration
**Evidence strength: mixed — mechanistically reasonable, limited direct RCT evidence for performance/durability.**

His backyard DNF pattern (feet destroyed, legs won't restart between laps) points to **distal fatigue-resilience, not aerobic limitation**. Relevant, but lower-certainty, interventions:
- **Foot intrinsic / "foot core" training:** weak plantar intrinsics are mechanistically linked to plantar fasciopathy, tibialis posterior tendinopathy, MTSS and Achilles issues, but direct evidence that training them prevents injury or improves ultra durability is limited. Low cost, reasonable to include (short-foot holds, towel curls, single-leg balance).
- **Tibialis posterior/anterior loading:** reasonable inference for a runner with distal breakdown; progressive resisted work plus single-leg balance (build to 3–4×60s single-leg stance, 2–3×/week).
- **Plyometric/stiffness work:** improves running economy at lower speeds (see 2.5) and builds tendon stiffness; must be introduced cautiously and only once the Achilles is quiet.
- **Running mechanics under extreme fatigue:** the specific adaptation for "legs won't restart" is best trained by durability (time on feet, back-to-back long runs) and strength endurance, plus rehearsing the walk/eat/restart transitions — this is as much a pacing/logistics problem as a physiological one.

## 1.6 Load management and injury risk: the honest version
**Evidence strength: the critiques are well-supported; simple rules are NOT well-supported.**

- **The "10% rule" is not evidence-based.** An RCT in novice runners found no injury-rate difference between a graded ~10%/week programme and faster progression; a 2018 systematic review found no evidence for a defined 10% threshold; a 2022 systematic review of 36 studies (23,047 runners) concluded the popular 10% rule "is not justified." Use it, if at all, as a loose default, not a law.
- **Acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) has been heavily criticised and should not be treated as settled.** Critiques (Impellizzeri et al.; Lolli et al.) cover mathematical coupling/ratio artefacts, the arbitrariness of the 0.8–1.3 "sweet spot," inconsistent and contradictory findings, and the fact that no study has shown that *applying* ACWR as an intervention actually reduces injuries. Some researchers have called for retraction of the original paper. Report it as contested, not as a target to hit.
- **What the evidence DOES support:** the strongest, most consistent risk factor is **previous injury** (directly relevant here) — established in multiple systematic reviews. Large recent data (Nielsen/Frandsen group, ~930-runner prospective cohort) point to **single-session spikes** — one overly long run relative to recent longest — mattering more than gradual weekly build. And **higher chronic training load is protective**: better-trained runners get injured less, so the goal is to build durable capacity, not to stay cautious forever.
- **Strength training is the best-evidenced prevention tool.** Lauersen et al. (BJSM 2014): strength training reduced overuse injuries by 47% (RR 0.527, 95% CI 0.373–0.746) and total injuries to under a third (RR 0.315); stretching did nothing (RR 0.96) — "strength training reduced sports injuries to less than 1/3 and overuse injuries could be almost halved." The 2018 follow-up found a dose-response: a 10% increase in strength-training volume gave a further >4-percentage-point drop in injury risk.

**Synthesis for his pattern (flares when volume and intensity rise together):** progress **one variable at a time**. When adding threshold/quality work, hold volume flat; when raising volume, keep it easy. Watch morning Achilles stiffness as the governing signal.

## 1.7 Concurrent training: strength and running together
**Evidence strength: well-supported that interference is small for recreational athletes.**

- The interference effect is real but minor at his volumes. Meta-analytic and review evidence shows session sequence has negligible effect on endurance and only a small effect on strength when sessions are separated.
- **Practical rules:** separate hard running and heavy lifting by ~6+ hours where possible, or put them on different days. If same-day and running quality matters most, run first. Note that lower-limb heavy strength can reduce running economy for up to ~6–8 hours afterwards, so don't do a hard run in the hours immediately after heavy legs.
- Given he cycles to/from the gym and trains twice weekly, the cleanest structure is to pair heavy lower-body lifting with an easy running day or a rest day, keeping it away from his key threshold and long-run sessions.

# PART TWO — FROM 3:13 TO SUB-3 AND THE SHARED ENDURANCE BASE

## 2.1 Training intensity distribution
**Evidence strength: well-supported that easy/hard polarisation beats grey-zone; polarised vs pyramidal is genuinely contested.**

His 2025–26 training is the textbook error: almost everything compressed into 4:45–5:15/km, very little genuinely easy and very little genuinely hard. The evidence is consistent that this "grey zone" clustering is the least productive way to distribute training.

What the evidence shows for recreational/sub-elite marathoners specifically:
- Recreational and elite marathoners who perform best follow a **pyramidal** distribution: a large base of easy running, a moderate amount of threshold, a little at high intensity. The largest analysis to date (Muniz-Pumares, Smyth et al., *Sports Medicine* 2024; 119,452 runners across 151,813 marathons) found that over 80% of runners with the fastest marathon times used a pyramidal TID, and that the proportion of easy (Zone 1) running was progressively higher in faster groups — the fastest devoted ~80% of mileage to easy running versus 50–60% for typical runners. **Easy-run volume is the single strongest differentiator between fast and average marathoners.**
- Both polarised and pyramidal beat threshold-clustered training; which of the two is superior is unsettled and appears individual. A 16-week RCT in recreational marathoners reported a polarised advantage; other work favours pyramidal for the marathon specifically. Do not present either as settled.

**How to define and control "easy" without lactate testing:**
- **Talk test** (can speak full sentences) — most practical, well-validated proxy for the aerobic threshold.
- **Heart rate:** roughly below ~75–80% of max HR; keep easy runs genuinely conversational.
- **Pace:** for him, easy is likely well slower than 5:15/km — probably 5:30–6:00/km or slower. This will feel "too slow"; that is the point.
- **RPE:** ≤3–4 out of 10.

Target roughly **80% easy / 20% moderate-to-hard by time**, structured as one to two quality sessions per week plus a long run, everything else easy.

## 2.2 Why longer threshold reps beat short fast intervals for the marathon
**Evidence strength: well-supported physiologically; his own data is a single-case confirmation.**

His 11-minute PB (3:24 → 3:13) coincided exactly with shifting from 400m/800m speed work to longer threshold reps (4×6min, 3×8min, threshold pyramids) at HM/threshold pace. This is what the physiology predicts:
- Marathon performance is governed by the fraction of VO2max sustainable, which is set largely by the **lactate threshold** — the strongest single physiological predictor of distance performance (Bassett & Howley). Threshold running trains the lactate production/clearance balance directly at an intensity specific to marathon demand.
- Short 400m/800m intervals develop VO2max and speed/economy but are further from marathon specificity and carry higher recovery cost per unit of marathon-relevant adaptation. Threshold work gives a large, specific return for moderate fatigue — a 30–40min tempo produces meaningful adaptation.
- LT1 (~marathon pace, ~2 mmol/L) and LT2 (~hour-race/HM pace, ~4 mmol/L) are distinct landmarks; marathon work should include both classic threshold (LT2) reps and longer marathon-pace (LT1) running.

**Recommendation:** make threshold the backbone of quality work (e.g. 4–5×6–8min, or 3×15min, at ~HM effort), reserving faster VO2max intervals for a smaller dose in the sharpening phase. Keep some speed, because 5k/10k economy makes marathon pace feel easier.

## 2.3 Weekly volume and the sub-3 requirement
**Evidence strength: well-supported association; individual requirement is inference.**

- Weekly mileage is a primary determinant of marathon time. Tanda (*Journal of Human Sport and Exercise* 2011;6(3):511–520; 22 runners, 46 races) found weekly mileage and mean training pace explained ~77% of marathon-finish-time variance in recreational runners, with diminishing returns above ~65 km/week.
- Sub-3 runners typically peak around 55–70+ miles/week (≈90–115 km) sustained across a 12–16 week build, with regular 30–35km long runs. Practitioner and cohort data (e.g. Humphrey) commonly cite average weeks of 55–60 miles and peaks of 65–70 for sub-3.
- His current 30–50 km (peaking 60–70) is short of that, and his engine (3:13 PB, 17:55 5k, 1:29 HM) suggests the limiter for sub-3 is **durability and specific volume, not raw speed**.

**The central tension:** sub-3 volume (~90–115 km/week) directly conflicts with a recurrent, never-properly-rehabbed Achilles. Resolution: build tendon capacity and a bigger easy base FIRST (next 3–6 months), so that when he runs the sub-3 block his tissues can tolerate 90+ km. Do not chase both volume and pace before the calf is loaded and capacity-tested.

## 2.4 Long-run design
**Evidence strength: reasonable inference; the "3-hour cap" is practitioner heuristic, not hard evidence.**

- The widely used cap of ~2.5–3 hours (or ~30–35km) reflects diminishing aerobic returns against rising musculoskeletal/recovery cost, but the "3-hour rule" is a **heuristic, not a firm evidence threshold** — some coaches and researchers argue duration should be individualised to durability, injury risk and fuelling.
- For marathon prep, long runs of ~2–2.5 hours, ~25–35km, done regularly, with the long run kept to ~25–30% of weekly volume, are well supported. His Florence build (24 → 30.6 → 26 → 34km, undulating rather than linear) is a sound template and produced his PB — worth replicating.
- **Fast-finish, progression, and marathon-pace segments within long runs** are well supported for marathon specificity and are higher-value than simply running longer. Insert MP blocks (e.g. last 40–60min at goal pace) rather than adding distance.
- Given his Achilles: cap single-run duration, insert walk breaks and softer surfaces, fuel aggressively (high carbohydrate intake reduces long-run breakdown), and protect the following days' recovery.

## 2.5 Strength training for endurance performance
**Evidence strength: well-supported for running economy; effect sizes small but real.**

- Heavy resistance training improves running economy with a small pooled effect (Eihara et al., *Sports Medicine Open* 2022 meta-analysis: g ≈ −0.32 for running economy, small; plyometrics trivial-to-small by comparison). Reported RE improvements commonly ~2–8% (Blagrove et al. 2018 systematic review).
- **Loading parameters with best evidence:** heavy loads (**≥80% 1RM**), multi-joint free-weight exercises (squat, deadlift variations), low-to-moderate reps (**~2–6 sets of 3–10 reps**), plus plyometrics for stiffness. High-load and combined (strength + plyometric) methods give the largest RE improvements; plyometrics help most at speeds <12 km/h.
- **Dose:** Blagrove's practical guidance — endurance athletes don't need to train near failure; ~60 minutes/week of focused S&C can drive meaningful gains; 2×/week is sufficient. Effects build over longer interventions (>8–12 weeks).
- **Periodisation alongside a marathon block:** develop maximal strength in the base phase; shift toward maintenance and more reactive/plyometric work in the specific phase; reduce strength volume (not intensity) during the taper. Strength can be **maintained on as little as one heavy session/week** during a race build.

This aligns perfectly with his two-gym-sessions-a-week constraint. His current numbers (squat 100kg single / 110×3 with a trainer, deadlift 6×100kg supervised) are a decent base; the missing piece is calf/Achilles-specific loading (Part One), not more upper body.

## 2.6 Periodisation without a fixed race date
**Evidence strength: reasonable inference from training principles + taper/block evidence.**

His constraint — 12–16 weeks' notice for a marathon — is well suited to a "maintain base, sharpen on demand" model:
- **Year-round base:** keep a permanent aerobic base of ~50–70km/week (as tolerated by the Achilles), mostly easy, with one steady threshold session and one long run weekly, plus 2× gym. This keeps him perpetually 12–16 weeks from race-ready and is also the most enjoyable, low-pressure structure — which suits his stated priorities.
- **What 12–16 weeks CAN do from a good base:** sharpen lactate threshold, build marathon-specific endurance and MP fitness, dial in fuelling, and taper. What it **cannot** do: build a large aerobic base from scratch or safely add tendon capacity that was never there — hence the base must be genuine year-round.
- **Essential marathon-specific work in the window:** progressive threshold → marathon-pace work; long runs with MP segments; race-fuelling and gut-training practice at MP; and a proper taper.

## 2.7 Tapering
**Evidence strength: well-supported (meta-analysis).**

Bosquet et al. (*Med Sci Sports Exerc* 2007;39(8):1358–65; meta-analysis of 27 studies) found the optimal taper reduces training **volume by ~41–60%**, **maintains intensity and frequency**, and lasts ~2 weeks (extend to ~3 weeks for the marathon given greater accumulated fatigue). The 41–60% volume cut produced a mean endurance improvement of ~2.2%, with runners ~2.6% faster than controls — several minutes for a 3-hour runner. Cutting volume by >60% is counter-productive. Keep short, sharp race-pace work through the taper — **reduce the length of quality sessions, not their pace**. Do not cut intensity or frequency.

## 2.8 Transferability to the 24-hour backyard ultra
**Evidence strength: reasonable inference; he already has direct experience.**

A marathon-oriented aerobic base transfers substantially — the aerobic engine, threshold, fat oxidation and calf/foot capacity all carry over. What is genuinely different, and where his DNFs actually occurred:
- **Durability over aerobic capacity:** the limiter is musculoskeletal (feet, calves, "legs won't restart"), not VO2max. This is built by time on feet, back-to-back long runs, and the lower-limb capacity work in Part One.
- **Pace is trivial; the skill is the transition** — eat, manage feet, restart each lap. His stomach and sleep were fine; the mechanical failure was distal. Prioritise calf/foot capacity, foot care/footwear, and rehearsing the between-lap routine.
- Keep this section brief in his system: he has three attempts of direct data, and the training that fixes his Achilles (calf loading, easy volume, strength) is the same training that most improves his backyard result.

# RECOMMENDATIONS (staged)

**Phase 0 — now to ~6 weeks (re-establish routine + start tendon work):**
1. Book a sports-physio assessment to confirm mid-portion vs insertional and rule out differentials. This gates the heavy heel-drop decision.
2. Start HSR calf loading 2–3×/week (bent-knee AND straight-knee), beginning ~15RM, 6-second reps. Baseline-test single-leg heel-raise both legs (reps, height, symmetry).
3. Rebuild easy running deliberately slow (talk-test pace, likely 5:30–6:00/km). One easy long run. Do NOT add intensity yet.
4. Governing signal: morning Achilles stiffness/first-steps pain; keep loading/running pain ≤5/10, settling by next morning, not climbing week to week.

**Phase 1 — ~6 weeks to ~4–6 months (build durable base):**
5. Progress HSR toward 6RM by week 12; retest heel-raise symmetry (target LSI ≥80–90%, using work/height not just reps).
6. Add ONE threshold session/week (start ~3×8–10min at HM effort, build to 3×15min / 4–5×8min). Hold volume flat when you add it.
7. Grow easy volume toward 60–70km/week, one variable at a time, watching the Achilles. Keep 2× gym (heavy lower body + calf, kept 6+ hours away from key runs).
8. Introduce foot/tibialis and light plyometric work once the tendon is quiet.

**Phase 2 — trigger on race announcement (12–16 week sub-3 block):**
9. Only start if he can tolerate ~70km/week pain-free and heel-raise symmetry is restored. If not, run the race as a "good day out," not a sub-3 attempt.
10. Pyramidal distribution ~80/20; backbone of threshold + marathon-pace long runs (MP segments, fast-finish); peak ~55–70km/week (push toward 90+ only if the Achilles clearly tolerates it).
11. Maintain strength at 1×/week heavy; add a small VO2max dose for economy.
12. 2.5–3 week taper: cut volume 40–60%, hold intensity and frequency. Practise fuelling at MP throughout the block, not just on race day.

**Benchmarks that change the plan:**
- Morning Achilles stiffness rising week-on-week → reduce load, hold volume, do not progress.
- Heel-raise symmetry <80% → not ready for a volume block; keep building capacity.
- Can't hold easy pace conversational → too fast; slow down regardless of the watch.
- 10k/HM time-trial not predicting sub-3 (needs roughly sub-38 10k / ~1:22–1:25 HM by VDOT) → extend the base phase rather than force the marathon block.

# CAVEATS
- **No diagnosis.** The Achilles has never been formally assessed; location (mid-portion vs insertional) materially changes exercise prescription and is not yet known. In-person clinical assessment is warranted before heavy heel-drop loading.
- **Marathon times are Strava moving time,** which flatters true finish/chip time and may slightly overstate fitness relative to the volume/pace benchmarks cited.
- **Much strength/economy and TID evidence comes from well-trained or elite athletes.** Effect sizes in a busy recreational runner around a full-time job will be at the smaller end, and adherence matters more than optimality — which he has correctly identified.
- **Controversies flagged honestly:** isometrics-for-pain is contested; ACWR is heavily criticised and not a target; the 10% rule is not evidence-based; polarised vs pyramidal is unresolved; the 3-hour long-run cap is a heuristic; heel-raise norms are protocol-dependent.
- **Enjoyment and consistency are the actual success variables here.** The evidence-optimal plan he won't follow is worse than a slightly sub-optimal plan he enjoys. Every recommendation above is deliberately compatible with a low-pressure, year-round, feel-good structure.
